about: Every fact in here names the source it came from. Nothing is written from memory and nothing is here without a place to go check it. Add a fact by adding a row to facts, and if it needs one, a row to sources. The published dates are the day each page first went up, taken from the repo history, and they are what the structured data says. Do not move one to make a page look newer.

towns.name: Graysville
towns.lede: The one that was never a company town. Graysville had the gin, and it kept a farm town's shape while its neighbors were being built around a mine shaft. It is also the only one of the three that has had to incorporate twice.

towns.name: Cardiff
towns.lede: Named by a Welshman for the place he came from, built on one mine, and burned down once. Cardiff has about five hundred fewer people now than it had the year it took its charter.

towns.name: Brookside
towns.lede: A Sloss company town that ended up with a Russian Orthodox parish, a Catholic parish, and 288 coke ovens, because the coal needed miners and the miners were in eastern Europe.

facts.title: The Crockers held it first
facts.note: The first settlers reached the Cardiff area in the 1830s, and the Crocker family held the land for the next fifty years while the coal underneath it sat there unbothered.

facts.title: Farms first, for fifty years
facts.note: The first settlers reached the bottomland here in 1838, and Brookside was farm country for close to fifty years before anybody opened a mine.

facts.title: Named for the water it sits on
facts.note: There is no Brookside family behind the name. It is a description of a town built beside Five Mile Creek, and that is all it has ever been.

facts.title: Sold to two men who wanted what was under it
facts.note: The Crockers sold in 1880 to Isaac Price and James Williamson, who opened the Cardiff mine. Price was Welsh and Williamson was Scottish, and they hired from home.

facts.title: Named for a town in Wales
facts.note: Price named the mine for Cardiff in Wales, and the town took the mine's name. It is one of four places in Jefferson County named for somewhere in Britain.

facts.title: They filled the town by letter
facts.note: Price and Williamson wrote to friends and family back in Wales offering them jobs. That is how Cardiff filled.

facts.title: Hired out of Wales, Scotland, France, and Italy
facts.note: Price and Williamson hired out of Wales and Scotland first, then France and Italy. Inside a few years Cardiff held several hundred families from across Europe.

facts.title: It was Gin Town before it was Graysville
facts.note: There was one cotton gin for miles and it was here, so Gin Town is what people called it. Who the Grays were, and when the name changed, nobody seems to have written down.

facts.title: The Brookside mine opens
facts.note: Coalburg Coal and Coke opened the mine in 1886. It ran thirty four years, and it is the reason there is a town here at all.

facts.title: Sloss buys it a year later
facts.note: Sloss Iron and Steel bought the Brookside mine in 1887 and burned its coal in the Birmingham furnaces.

facts.title: Sloss went to Europe for miners
facts.note: Sloss could not find enough skilled miners here, so its recruiters went to the Austro Hungarian Empire. Slovak and Carpatho Rusyn families arrived through the 1890s.

facts.title: Stewarts, Woodfords, Negrons, Tombrellos
facts.note: The Stewarts came from Scotland, the Woodfords from Wales, the Negrons from France, and the Tombrellos from Sicily. The marker in town lists them by name.

facts.title: St. Nicholas is founded
facts.note: The parish was founded in 1894, one of the first Russian Orthodox congregations south of the Mason and Dixon line. The building standing there today came later.

facts.title: And the Catholic parish the year after
facts.note: SS. Cyril and Methodius followed in 1895. Two churches inside two years, in a town not yet ten years old.

facts.title: Graysville takes its charter
facts.note: Graysville incorporated in 1897, the first of the three to do it.

facts.title: A coal washer at the mine
facts.note: The Robinson Ramsey washer went in at Brookside in 1897, which put the mine ahead of most of what was operating around it.

facts.title: The Primrose won the state cup
facts.note: The Welsh and Scottish miners at Cardiff put together a football club and called it the Primrose. In 1898 it won the Alabama Foot Ball Association Cup.

facts.title: Brookside takes its charter
facts.note: Brookside incorporated in 1898, twelve years after the mine opened.

facts.title: Cardiff takes its charter
facts.note: Cardiff incorporated in January 1900 with more than 560 people, several stores, two blacksmith shops, and a saloon.

facts.title: A depot, a drugstore, and several saloons
facts.note: By 1900 Brookside had a railroad depot, dry goods stores, a drugstore, and more than one saloon. Its first school went up the same year and was replaced in 1923.

facts.title: 288 beehive coke ovens
facts.note: Sloss ran 288 domed brick ovens at Brookside, built shoulder to shoulder so they would hold each other's heat and charged through a hole in the roof.

facts.title: One church for everybody
facts.note: The Union Church went up a street over from downtown Graysville. It was the only church for miles, so every denomination met in it.

facts.title: Better than a third of the town was Slovak
facts.note: By 1910 Slovak families made up roughly 37 percent of Brookside.

facts.title: Two dollars and fifty cents a year for the roads
facts.note: Cardiff put on a street tax of $2.50 a year in 1911, and the road work it paid for ran on until 1946.

facts.title: Machines take over from the pick
facts.note: Mechanical cutters replaced hand picks at the Brookside mine in 1913.

facts.title: Six hundred men underground
facts.note: The Brookside mine employed over 600 men in 1914, the most it ever had. Four years before that it had been down to 54.

facts.title: The church you can still go see
facts.note: The St. Nicholas building was finished in 1916 and re-faced in brick in 1965. It still puts on a Russian and Slavic food festival the first full weekend in November.

facts.title: Downtown burns
facts.note: Cardiff's downtown burned on July 20, 1919, and the town's fortunes turned down with it.

facts.title: The mine closes and never reopens
facts.note: A United Mine Workers strike and a worldwide collapse in coal prices shut the Brookside mine in 1920. The strike was settled in 1921 and the mine never went back to work.

facts.title: The ovens come down
facts.note: Sloss opened a by-product coke plant in North Birmingham in 1920 and took the Brookside ovens apart. The Library of Congress holds a photographic record of what was left.

facts.title: The state pulls the charter
facts.note: Alabama revoked Graysville's charter in 1927 on the grounds of inactivity. For the next eighteen years there was no town government here.

facts.title: The lights come on
facts.note: Alabama Power brought electricity to Brookside in 1927, seven years after the mine that built the town had closed.

facts.title: From 562 people down to 146
facts.note: Cardiff counted 562 in 1900 and 146 in 1930. Underground mining was going out, and strip mining did not need a town around it.

facts.title: Back on the map, for the water
facts.note: Graysville reincorporated on November 17, 1945, mainly so it could build and run its own water system.

facts.title: The first council meets in the old schoolhouse
facts.note: The new council held its first meeting on January 16, 1946, in the old schoolhouse.

facts.title: Then the gas board
facts.note: Graysville set up a gas board in 1949. It is the Municipal Gas System now.

facts.title: Brookside builds a city hall
facts.note: Brookside put up its city hall in 1953.

facts.title: A town hall, a jail, and a fire station
facts.note: Graysville built all three across the 1950s.

facts.title: The subdivisions go in
facts.note: Mines and steel mills drew families from all over Alabama, and Graysville laid out its first subdivisions to hold them.

facts.title: Graysville peaks at 2,870
facts.note: The 1960 census found 2,870 people in Graysville, more than any count before or since. Families had moved in for work in the mines and the steel mills.

facts.title: Brookside peaks at 1,409
facts.note: Brookside's highest count came in 1980, sixty years after the mine closed.

facts.title: It grew by annexing the county
facts.note: Graysville took in unincorporated county land through the 1980s and 1990s. It covers 16.07 square miles now, about seventy six times the size of Cardiff.

facts.title: Six cities go in together
facts.note: Six cities formed a district in 2002 to clean up Five Mile Creek and open it back up to people. Graysville and Brookside are two of them.

facts.title: The 2003 flood
facts.note: Storms in May 2003 put Five Mile Creek through Cardiff and destroyed a number of buildings near the water.

facts.title: Ten inches in ten hours
facts.note: The same run of storms in 2003 dropped ten inches of rain in ten hours and put water through downtown Brookside.

facts.title: The marker goes up
facts.note: The Alabama Tourism Department and the Town of Cardiff put up a marker on the history in May 2010. A good deal of what this page says about Cardiff is on it.

facts.title: Named an Alabama Community of Excellence
facts.note: Graysville entered the program in the class of 2007 and was designated in 2011.

facts.title: The EF3
facts.note: An EF3 tornado came through Graysville on January 23, 2012.

facts.title: The greenway joins Red Rock
facts.note: The Five Mile Creek Greenway became part of the area wide Red Rock Ridge and Valley Trail System in 2012.

facts.title: Sixteen and a half miles of railroad
facts.note: In July 2018 the six cities and the Freshwater Land Trust bought 16.5 miles of corridor from CSX. It was laid in the late 1800s as part of the Birmingham Mineral Railroad, to haul coal out of mines like the ones at Cardiff and Brookside.

facts.title: Fifty two people
facts.note: The 2020 census counted 52 people in Cardiff, on 0.21 square miles. In 1900 it was 562.

facts.title: The police department and the lawsuit
facts.note: Brookside's police chief resigned on January 25, 2022. In February 2026 the town agreed to pay $1.5 million to settle a civil rights lawsuit.

facts.title: The longest trail in the county
facts.note: An extension that opened in 2023 made the Five Mile Creek Greenway the longest multiuse trail in Jefferson County.

ovens-working.caption: The Brookside ovens working, behind the depot. The handwriting is on the print itself.
ovens-working.alt: A long bank of brick coke ovens built into a hillside with smoke rising from several of them, and a line of open rail cars standing on an elevated trestle above. Handwriting on the print reads Brookside Coke Ovens in Bside, and Back of Brookside Depot.

brookside-siteplan.credit: Historic American Engineering Record, Library of Congress
brookside-siteplan.caption: The mine that opened here in 1886, measured and drawn in the summer of 1992, long after the last of it stopped working. The two long curves following the hillside are the coke oven batteries.
brookside-siteplan.alt: A large archival measured drawing headed Brookside Coal Mine and Beehive Coke Ovens, Jefferson County, Alabama. A site plan across the top shows two long curved batteries of coke oven ruins following the contours of a hillside above Mount Olive Road, with four mine openings and abandoned rail beds marked. A second drawing below plots the surviving foundations of the tipple, crusher, washer and coal storage bins.

chapters.title: Before the coal

big.line: Both places were farm country for about fifty years before anybody opened a mine.

chapters.blurb: It is easy to assume the coal was always the point here. For about fifty years it was not. Two of the three towns already had people living in them, and neither of them had any reason yet to be a town.
chapters.summary: It is easy to look at these three places now and assume the coal was always the point. For about fifty years it was not. The first settlers reached the Cardiff area in the 1830s, and the Crocker family held that land for the next fifty years with the coal sitting underneath it, unbothered and unremarked on. Brookside was farm bottomland from 1838, and it stayed farm country for close to fifty years before anybody opened a mine. Even the name is plain. There is no Brookside family behind it and there never was, only a description of a town built beside a creek. What this chapter holds is farmland with something valuable underneath it that nobody had yet decided to go and get, which is worth keeping in mind when you read what happens next.
chapters.note: Farms on the bottomland and a cotton gin. Two of the three already had people in them and neither had a reason to be a town yet.

chapters.title: The camps

big.line: Cardiff opened its mine in 1880 and Brookside opened its in 1886, and almost everything about both towns follows from that.

chapters.blurb: Cardiff went first. Two men bought the land in 1880, opened a mine, named it for home, and then filled the town by writing letters to Wales. Six years later Brookside did the same thing on a larger scale, and Sloss money was behind it inside a year.
chapters.summary: Everything that follows starts here, and it starts with a sale. The Crockers sold in 1880 to Isaac Price and James Williamson, two men who wanted what was under the land rather than the land itself. Price was Welsh and Williamson was Scottish, they opened the Cardiff mine, and Price named it for Cardiff in Wales, which is how one of four places in Jefferson County came to be named for somewhere in Britain. Then they did the thing that shaped the town more than the mine did. They wrote home. Price and Williamson sent letters to friends and family in Wales offering them work, hired out of Scotland next and then France and Italy, and inside a few years Cardiff held several hundred families from across Europe. Brookside's mine opened in 1886 under Coalburg Coal and Coke and ran for thirty four years, and Sloss Iron and Steel bought it in 1887 and started burning its coal in the Birmingham furnaces. Graysville was doing none of this. It had one cotton gin, no company behind it, and a name people used for it that was not its own, which was Gin Town.
chapters.note: Cardiff goes first. Two men buy the land, open a mine, name it for home, and start writing letters to Wales. Six years later Brookside does the same thing on a larger scale with Sloss money behind it.

chapters.title: Charters and churches

big.line: Brookside founded St. Nicholas in 1894 and SS. Cyril and Methodius in 1895, in a town not yet ten years old.

chapters.blurb: This is the decade the camps became towns. All three took a charter inside ten years, and the families filling Brookside's houses had come from the far side of the Austro Hungarian Empire to do it.
chapters.summary: This is the decade the camps turned into towns, and it happened on two fronts at once. Sloss could not find enough skilled miners in Alabama, so its recruiters went to the Austro Hungarian Empire, and Slovak and Carpatho Rusyn families arrived in Brookside through the 1890s. At Cardiff the names had come from further west: the Stewarts from Scotland, the Woodfords from Wales, the Negrons from France, and the Tombrellos from Sicily, all of them listed by name on the marker that stands in town today. Those families built what they had come from. St. Nicholas was founded in 1894, one of the first Russian Orthodox congregations south of the Mason and Dixon line, and SS. Cyril and Methodius followed in 1895, which is two churches inside two years in a town that was not yet ten years old. The paperwork caught up at the same time. Graysville incorporated in 1897 and was the first of the three to do it, Brookside followed in 1898 twelve years after its mine opened, and the Robinson Ramsey coal washer that went in at Brookside in 1897 put the mine ahead of most of what was operating around it.
chapters.note: Inside ten years all three take a charter, Brookside builds two churches, and Cardiff wins a state cup. This is the decade the camps turn into towns.

chapters.title: The peak

big.line: The Brookside mine employed more than six hundred men in 1914, the most it ever had.

chapters.blurb: For twenty years the valley ran at full tilt. Nearly everything these three towns still get measured against was built, counted, or finished inside these twenty years, which is also why the decade ends the way it does.
chapters.summary: By 1914 there were more than six hundred men going underground at Brookside every morning, which is worth sitting with for a second, because four years before that the same mine had been down to fifty four. On the hillside above them Sloss ran 288 domed brick ovens, built shoulder to shoulder so they would hold each other's heat and charged through a hole in the roof. A town grew to serve all of it. By 1900 Brookside had a railroad depot, dry goods stores, a drugstore, and more than one saloon, and its first school went up that same year. Cardiff took its charter in January 1900 with more than 560 people, several stores, two blacksmith shops, and a saloon of its own, and in 1911 it put on a street tax of two dollars and fifty cents a year that paid for road work all the way to 1946. By 1910 Slovak families made up roughly 37 percent of Brookside, and in 1916 that community finished the St. Nicholas building you can still go and see. Nearly everything these three towns still get measured against was built, counted, or finished inside these twenty years, which is also why the last entry lands the way it does. Cardiff's downtown burned on 20 July 1919, and the town's fortunes turned down with it.
chapters.note: Depots, schools, saloons, six hundred men underground and 288 ovens burning. Nearly everything these towns still get measured against happened in these twenty years.

chapters.title: The mine closes

big.line: A strike and a worldwide collapse in the coal price shut the Brookside mine, and it never went back to work.

chapters.blurb: It ended inside a year. The mine that built Brookside closed in 1920 and never reopened, the ovens came down, and seven years later the state took Graysville's charter away.
chapters.summary: Thirty four years of work stopped inside a single year. A United Mine Workers strike and a worldwide collapse in coal prices shut the Brookside mine in 1920, and although the strike was settled in 1921 the mine never went back to work. Sloss had already moved on. It opened a by-product coke plant in North Birmingham that same year and took the Brookside ovens apart, and the photographic record the Library of Congress holds of what was left is most of what there is to look at now. Graysville lost something different, and lost it for a different reason. Alabama revoked its charter in 1927 on the grounds of inactivity, and for the next eighteen years there was no town government there at all. The one thing that arrived rather than left in this decade arrived late. Alabama Power brought electricity to Brookside in 1927, seven years after the mine that built the town had already closed.
chapters.note: A strike and a collapse in the coal price end it inside a year. Brookside loses the mine and gets electricity seven years later. Graysville loses its charter outright.

chapters.title: After the coal

big.line: Graysville's 1960 census count, the highest any of the three towns has ever recorded.

chapters.blurb: Seventy years in one chapter, because the three spent it going three different ways. Cardiff emptied out, Graysville came back from the dead and grew, and Brookside held on and reached its own high water mark in 1980.
chapters.summary: Seventy years is a lot to put in one chapter, and it belongs in one because the three towns spent it going three different directions. Cardiff emptied. It had counted 562 people in 1900 and counted 146 in 1930, because underground mining was going out and strip mining did not need a town around it. Graysville did the opposite, and did it on purpose. It reincorporated on 17 November 1945 mainly so it could build and run its own water system, held its first council meeting in the old schoolhouse that January, set up a gas board in 1949 that is the Municipal Gas System today, and built a town hall, a jail, and a fire station across the 1950s. Mines and steel mills were drawing families in from all over Alabama, so Graysville laid out its first subdivisions to hold them, and the 1960 census found 2,870 people there, more than any count before or since. Through the 1980s and 1990s it kept growing by annexing unincorporated county land, which is why it covers 16.07 square miles now, about seventy six times the size of Cardiff. Brookside did neither of those things. It put up a city hall in 1953 and reached its own highest count, 1,409 people, in 1980, sixty years after the mine closed.
chapters.note: Seventy years in one chapter, because the three went in three directions. Cardiff emptied out, Graysville reincorporated and grew, Brookside held on.

chapters.title: The creek comes back

big.line: The corridor six cities and the Freshwater Land Trust bought from CSX in 2018, laid in the late 1800s to haul this coal out.

chapters.blurb: The water that carried the mine waste is the thing being cleaned up and walked along now, and the rail bed that hauled the coal out is the trail. None of which has stopped the creek flooding, and 2003 is still the year people here measure a storm against.
chapters.summary: The story turns around in this chapter, and the thing that turns it is the creek. Six cities formed a district in 2002 to clean up Five Mile Creek and open it back up to people, and Graysville and Brookside are two of them. In 2012 the Five Mile Creek Greenway became part of the area wide Red Rock Ridge and Valley Trail System, and in July 2018 the six cities and the Freshwater Land Trust bought 16.5 miles of corridor from CSX. That corridor was laid in the late 1800s as part of the Birmingham Mineral Railroad, to haul coal out of mines like the ones at Cardiff and Brookside, which means the road built to take the coal away is the path people walk on now, and an extension that opened in 2023 made it the longest multiuse trail in Jefferson County. None of that makes the water tame. Storms in May 2003 put Five Mile Creek through Cardiff and destroyed a number of buildings near it, and the same run of storms dropped ten inches of rain in ten hours and put water through downtown Brookside. The rest of the chapter is the ordinary business of small towns carrying on. A marker went up in Cardiff in May 2010 that a good deal of this page depends on, Graysville was named an Alabama Community of Excellence in 2011 and took an EF3 tornado through it in January 2012, the 2020 census counted 52 people in Cardiff where there had once been 562, and Brookside's police chief resigned in January 2022 in a matter the town settled in February 2026 for $1.5 million.
chapters.note: The water that carried the mine waste is the thing being cleaned up and walked along now, and the rail bed that hauled the coal out is the trail.
